content: 1. Rosas and colleagues conducted a study in Brazil examining the role of conscientious objection, barriers, and abortion in cases of rape, highlighting the perspectives of physicians. 2. Fink et al. explored the attitudes of physician conscientious objectors in Bogotá, Colombia, regarding abortion and referral practices, emphasizing the dual consideration of the fetus as a patient. 3. The Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted by the United Nations in 1989, establishes the rights of children globally. 4. General Comment No. 6 by the United Nations Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2018) addresses equality and non-discrimination principles. 5. The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), adopted in 1979, outlines measures to ensure women's rights and eliminate discrimination. 6. The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) released revised international technical guidance on sexuality education, emphasizing evidence-informed approaches. 7. The World Health Organization (WHO) issued a statement on preventing and eliminating disrespect and abuse during facility-based childbirth. 8. Norris et al. reconceptualized abortion stigma, analyzing its constituents, causes, and consequences in the context of women's health issues. 9. Hanschmidt et al. conducted a systematic review on abortion stigma, providing insights into its prevalence and impact on sexual and reproductive health. 10. Kumar and colleagues conceptualized abortion stigma, exploring its cultural, health, and social dimensions. 11. The WHO's framework for strengthening health systems aims to improve health outcomes through integrated and people-centered services. 12. Universal health coverage (UHC) for sexual and reproductive health is supported by evidence briefs and WHO's compendium of resources. 13. Coast et al. analyzed the microeconomic consequences of abortion care, focusing on the financial impact on individuals seeking abortion services. 14. Lattof and colleagues examined the mesoeconomic effects of abortion on health systems, analyzing resource allocation and service delivery. 15. Rodgers et al. reviewed the macroeconomic costs and outcomes of abortion, providing a comprehensive analysis of its broader economic implications. 16. Cook, Dickens, and Fathalla integrated medicine, ethics, and law in their work on reproductive health and human rights. 17. Billings et al. documented efforts to construct access to legal abortion services in Mexico City, highlighting partnerships and practical strategies. 18. Villela and Araújo described the implementation of legal abortion services in Brazil, emphasizing collaborative approaches. 19. Cook and Ngwena analyzed the legal framework governing women's access to healthcare, focusing on reproductive rights. 20. Cook et al. discussed prenatal management of anencephaly, addressing ethical and medical considerations. 21. Lavelanet et al. provided a descriptive analysis of global abortion policies, examining regulatory and policy environments. 22. Assifi et al. synthesized evidence on abortion care pathways for adolescents in high-income countries, identifying service provision challenges. 23. Iyengar and Iyengar shared experiences with manual vacuum aspiration as a primary health service for elective abortion in rural India. 24. Cook et al. emphasized the importance of transparency in implementing abortion laws, advocating for clear guidelines and accountability. 25. Coast et al. proposed a conceptual framework for understanding women's trajectories in abortion-related care. 26. Mundigo and Indriso explored abortion in the developing world, addressing cultural, social, and healthcare challenges. 27. The United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women issued concluding observations on Portugal's compliance with CEDAW. 28. Dzakpasu et al. systematically reviewed the impact of user fees on maternal health service utilization and outcomes. 29. The United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women provided observations on Germany's adherence to women's rights. 30. The WHO's 2006 World Health Report emphasized collaboration to improve global health outcomes. 31. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine outlined essential clinical competencies for abortion providers in the United States. 32. The WHO developed a global competency framework for universal health coverage, focusing on integrated health services. 33. The WHO's model list of essential medicines includes updates to ensure access to critical health products. 34. Babigumira et al. proposed a risk-based framework for pharmaceutical quality assurance in lowand middle-income countries. 35. The WHO's Global Abortion Policies Database provides comprehensive information on abortion regulations and policies worldwide. 36. Mutua et al. examined the intersection of policy, law, and post-abortion care services in Kenya. 37. Rehfuss et al. integrated WHO norms and values into a complexity perspective for health policy development. 38. Schünemann et al. edited the GRADE handbook, a tool for assessing evidence quality and recommendation strength. 39. The WHO published guidelines on the medical management of abortion, emphasizing evidence-based practices. 40. The WHO's clinical practice handbook for safe abortion provides practical guidance for healthcare providers. 41. Rodek and Deans discussed red cell alloimmunization in the context of fetal medicine and clinical practice. 42. Wiebe et al. compared Rh alloimmunization practices in Canada and the Netherlands, questioning the necessity of routine testing in early abortions. 43. The WHO issued recommendations on antenatal care to promote a positive pregnancy experience. 44. Penney et al. conducted a randomized comparison of strategies to reduce infectious complications of induced abortion. 45. Duncan et al. evaluated the utility of routine ultrasound for detecting ectopic pregnancies among women seeking abortion. 46. Smith et al. quantified pain during first-trimester abortion and its relationship with other variables. 47. Bélanger et al. studied psychosocial and medical predictors of pain during first-trimester abortion. 48. Renner et al. reviewed pain control methods for first-trimester surgical abortion. 49. Borgotta and Nickinovich analyzed pain experiences during early abortion procedures. 50. Grimes et al. proposed measures to prevent uterine perforation during curettage abortion. 51. Schulz et al. recommended strategies to prevent cervical injury during suction curettage abortion. 52. The WHO's recommendations on task shifting aim to optimize health worker roles to improve access to maternal and newborn health interventions. 53. The United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women issued concluding observations on Croatia's compliance with CEDAW. 54. The WHO's recommendations on misoprostol use for treating missed abortion in the first trimester provide evidence-based guidance. 55. Lemmers et al. reviewed medical treatments for early fetal death, focusing on efficacy and safety. 56. Lähteenmäki and Luukkainen studied the return of ovarian function after abortion. 57. Schreiber et al. examined ovulation resumption following medical abortion with mifepristone and misoprostol. 58. Kim et al. conducted a systematic review on initiating systemic hormonal contraception after abortion. 59. The WHO issued guidance on ensuring human rights in the provision of contraceptive information and services. 60. Raymond et al. investigated the timing of depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injection and its effects on medical abortion efficacy. 61. De Roodenbeke et al. explored outreach services as a strategy to increase access to health workers in remote areas. 62. Haemmerli et al. assessed the equity of social franchising in maternal healthcare in Uganda and India. 63. The WHO's report on eHealth highlights its role in achieving universal health coverage.
